segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I would like to talk a little bit more about writing in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, we haven't really looked so much about how to read and write in Spanish. We've spelled some words, we've discussed some sounds, and we've looked at convertible words, convertible, words that we convert over from Latin English into Spanish, and they give us a great idea about how to read and write in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, if we have a "j" sound, no, for example in general, how is this pronounced in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: General.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: General, and it's spelled the same. So there we understand that "g-e" makes "je" sound.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Without having to learn it formally, we can just look back to these convertible words when we are unsure of how a sound might be pronounced. So maybe you see "c-e" together and you're like is that "ce" or is that "que"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But then if you look back to concentración, then you have your answer. Concen- c-e, concentración, gives you your answer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So apart from the actual sounds, we also need to understand where the stress in any given word is when we read it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in Spanish, you may have noticed you have written accents, little dashes above some vowels.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, this isn't like French, for example, where the little dashes might actually change the sound of the vowel. None of that, luckily, is going on in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The written accent is just showing the stress. But why do we have it sometimes and not other times?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there is a general rule in Spanish, which is: If the word ends in a vowel, an "n", or an "s", the accent should be on the penultimate syllable, on the second-last syllable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, why do you think vowels and then "n"s and "s"s have been singled out for that rule?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What if you look at our verbs? What do our verb forms end in?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The they end in an "n".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah yes, "s" as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vowel.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. So it's what our verbs end in: in "n", "s", or vowel.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So Spanish says, if a word ends in "n", "s", or vowel, the natural accent will be on the penultimate syllable, the second-last syllable: diferente, habla, hablan, hablas, hablamos...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ending "s", but we're adding two syllables, so it's still on the second-last: hablamos,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: importante, adictivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if the word ends in any other consonant, any other consonant that's not "n" or "s", then the natural accent place is to go to the end of the word, and we see this perfectly with any "to" verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No? How do you say "to eat"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Accent on the end: comer. "To be" for states?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estar. "To speak"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablar. "To find"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encontrar. So this "r" is not an "n" or an "s" or a vowel, and what that means is that the accent is coming on the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So these are our natural accents. And if the word obeys the rules of the natural accents, we have no written accent, generally. There's a couple of exceptions which I'll mention.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if there's no written accent, you follow those rules. If it ends "n", "s", or vowel, you put the accent on the second-last syllable, and if it ends in any other consonant, you're putting the accent on the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if your word breaks this rule, then you have a written accent to show you where you should be stressing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, what is "tradition" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tradición.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tradición. And what are you ending it with? What is the last letter?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And where is the accent?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: At the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: At the end. Does this break our rule?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the "o" will have a written accent, that last "o" will have a written accent on the end showing you that you're stressing it: tradición.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So all of these -ción words that all have their accent on the end, situación, opinión, they all have a written accent there on the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now I'm going to tell you some words that we've come across already, and I want you to tell me if they will have a written accent or not. So what you need to decide is, are they breaking the accent rule or not?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encuentro. Encuentro. Firstly, what does that mean, encuentro?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I encounter.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, I find. Encuentro. Do we have a written accent there?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, good. Encontró. What does that mean first, encontró?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I uh sorry, he, she, it or you formal found.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And does it have a written accent?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, because it's breaking the rule. We're ending in a vowel and we have the accent on the end. So all of these in that point in the past are going to have that accent: encontró, habló, llamó, llegó. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vive. Vive. Firstly, what does that mean, vive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He, she, it, you formal live.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Does it have an accent?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Vivió.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It has an accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Where?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: At the "o".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Vivió. He lived, she lived, you formal lived, it lived.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Limón. What do you think limón means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lemon?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lemon, good, which is a Persian word actually, and and it actually was used to talk about citrus fruits generically, generally, and lime came from the same word, so lemon and lime is actually the same word essentially.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Does it have an accent, limón?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, because it should be "limon", right? But it's not, it's limón, it's breaking that rule, so it has a written accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when we're reading Spanish, if the word ends in a vowel, an "n", or an "s", we want to put the accent on the penultimate syllable. If it ends in another consonant, we want to put the accent on the end, unless we are shown with a written accent that the rule is being broken.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salud means "health", related to salute in English. Salud, and you can say it when you toast.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Does it have a written accent?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, good. It ends in a "d", so we expect the accent to be on the end: salud.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So usually accents are written to show us that we're breaking the accent rule. But there are some other situations where we have a written accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: One of these situations is when we have words that are monosyllables, words that are just one syllable, and we can differentiate them with a written accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, how was the word for "yes"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And how was the word for "if"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Si.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Si. It's the same word. So "yes" is written with a written accent,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and "if" is not. Now this written accent doesn't change the pronunciation. It just differentiates them so when you're reading you don't have the ambiguity that could sometimes be caused by, "Oh, is that a yes or an if?" Both could make sense there.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Especially because you use "yes" emphatically in Spanish. You can say "sí lo quiero" - "yes, I want it", but if that's written and you don't hear the emphasis, "si lo quiero", then you might read "if I want it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to clear up that ambiguity, when you have monosyllables, words of one syllable that are the same, one will take an accent to show the difference.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How was "for me"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Para mí or por mí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, very good, either one depending what "for" we want.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, how was "my house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mi casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mi casa. So this is different "mi".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: One is the the "mí" that comes after prepositions: para mí, por mí, de mí, and the other one is for possession: my.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So para mí, there you have the written accent on the "mí" of para mí, and you don't have it on mi casa, just to show the difference.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for "you", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tú.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tú. And what was "your house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tu casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tu casa. The word for "you", tú, takes a written accent, but the word for "your" in "your house", tu casa, doesn't.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So monosyllables that are the same are differentiated by accent. "I know", how do you say "I know"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sé.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. This sé has a written accent. The se of se lo doy, I give it to him, the se of se queda, he remains himself, she remains herself, doesn't have an accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Only the sé of saber, "I know", has one. So it's something you will pick up reading.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another example where we have accents is to differentiate question words from non-question words when they're the same.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, you have donde, what does donde mean?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Where.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Where. But sometimes dónde is a question word, like ¿dónde estás?, "where are you?", there it will go with an accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if I say "I'm going to meet him where we saw the football", this is not a question,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: so it doesn't have an accent. So Spanish likes to differentiate them as well. But now we're entering quite a bit of detail and many Spanish speakers when they're writing make these mistakes as well and don't put these accents where they should.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But I'm explaining just in case you come across dónde with an accent and you don't understand why it's there because it's not breaking the accent rule, this is why.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in the same way, we have como, which means "how" or "like". The cómo for "how" takes an accent, and the como for "like" doesn't.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there are a couple of grammatical examples when we are having accents just to differentiate words that are the same or to differentiate question words from non-question words, but most of the time they are directing us to break the accenting rules.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And it's very easy to remember the accenting rules because we only need to look at the present tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We know that our verbs end in vowels, "n"s or "s"s, and in the present tense we always have the accent on the penultimate syllable, without any written accent,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: with of course that one exception, estar, where we have estás, están, está, and we do have a written accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can look back there at the present tense to remind us that if the word ends "n", "s", or vowel, the natural accent is on the penultimate syllable like the verbs in the present tense, and if it ends in any other letter, the natural accent is on the end of the word.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And if we break this rule, we show it with a written accent.
